title: Descriptive Statistics
body:
Everything in [[STATISTICS]] after block 1 is inference: claims about a population you did not
measure. **Descriptive statistics is the part that claims nothing.** You have numbers, you
summarise and draw them, and every statement is a fact about the data in front of you. Doing it
first is not a formality: the shape of the data decides which later tool is legal, and a histogram
catches the bimodal distribution or the transcription error that would have silently wrecked a
$t$-test.

## Sample versus population

**This is the distinction the whole course runs on.** A *population* is every unit you care about;
a *sample* is the subset you actually measured. A number computed from the population is a
**parameter** and is usually unknowable; the same number computed from a sample is a **statistic**
and is what you have.

| Quantity | Population (parameter) | Sample (statistic) |
|---|:-:|:-:|
| [[Mean]] | $\mu$ | $\bar{x}$ |
| [[Variance]] | $\sigma^2$ | $s^2$ |
| Standard deviation | $\sigma$ | $s$ |
| Proportion | $p$ | $\hat{p}$ |
| Size | $N$ | $n$ |

Greek for what you want, Roman for what you measured. The convention is worth internalising
because formulas change depending on which side you are on: the population [[Variance]] divides by
$N$ and the sample one divides by $n - 1$, and that is not a typo.

**How the sample was drawn matters more than how big it is.** A simple random sample gives every
unit an equal chance. Stratified sampling splits the population into groups and samples within
each, which is the same idea as [[Stratification]] in a train/test split. A sample that selects
itself (survey responses, online reviews) is biased no matter how large, and no amount of
arithmetic downstream repairs it.

## Data classification

The type of the data decides which summary and which plot are even defined.

| Type | Meaning | Example | Mean defined? |
|---|---|---|:-:|
| Qualitative (categorical) | labels, no arithmetic | eye colour, course code | no, only [[Mode]] |
| Quantitative discrete | countable values | number of defects, dice roll | yes |
| Quantitative continuous | any value in an interval | height, time to failure | yes |

The discrete/continuous split reappears immediately in block 2 as the split between a
[[Probability Distribution|mass function]] and a [[Probability Density Function|density]], and it
is the same distinction: countable outcomes you sum over versus an interval you integrate over.
Compare [[Discrete]] and [[Continuous]] in COMP 2659, which draw the same line for signals.

## Graphical displays

- **Histogram**: bin the range, height is the count per bin. The workhorse. It shows centre,
  spread, skew, and modality in one picture, and the bin width is a real choice (too wide hides
  structure, too narrow shows noise).
- **Frequency polygon**: the histogram's bin midpoints joined by lines. Useful mainly for
  overlaying two distributions, which stacked bars do badly.
- **Stem-and-leaf**: the histogram's shape with the original digits kept, so nothing is lost. A
  hand-drawn tool, and it is the only one of the four you can reverse back into the raw data.
- **Boxplot**: the five-number summary drawn as a box. Median line, box from $Q_1$ to $Q_3$
  (the interquartile range), whiskers to the furthest point within $1.5 \times \text{IQR}$, and
  anything past that plotted individually as an **outlier**. The box holds the middle half of the
  data by construction.

**Skew is read off the picture, not the numbers.** A right-skewed histogram has its tail to the
right and its [[Mean]] pulled that way, so $\text{mode} < \text{median} < \text{mean}$. Left-skew
reverses it, and a symmetric distribution collapses all three onto the same point. Boxplots show
the same thing as an off-centre median line.

## What to report

The two-number summary is a centre plus a spread, and they have to be chosen as a pair:

| Data looks like | Centre | Spread |
|---|---|---|
| roughly symmetric, no outliers | [[Mean]] | standard deviation |
| skewed, or has outliers | [[Median]] | interquartile range |
| categorical | [[Mode]] | frequency table |

Reporting a mean with no measure of spread is the most common failure in the whole subject. Two
datasets with identical means can be a tight cluster and a bimodal split, and the mean is the same
lie in both cases.

## Related

- [[Average Value]]: the index into the three centre measures
- [[Variance]]: spread, and why the sample formula divides by $n - 1$
- [[Sampling Distribution]]: what happens when you compute $\bar{x}$ over and over from fresh
  samples, which is where description stops and inference starts
- [[Linear Regression]]: a scatter diagram is the two-variable version of this block
- [[Principal Component Analysis]] (MATH 2303): exploratory analysis for data with too many columns
  to plot, and it is built from the covariance of exactly these summaries
